# Chapter 1 · The Promise at the Front Door

> **Inputs:** none. This is where the story starts.
> **Code:** `src/itsdangerous/__init__.py`, `README.md`, `docs/index.rst`, `docs/concepts.rst`

You are about to put your name on a library that stands between your application and forged sessions. Before reading a line of the signing code, it is worth knowing how big the thing is, what it says it does, and — just as importantly — what it never claims to do.

Start with size. The entire public surface of `itsdangerous` is one file, and that file does nothing but re-export.

## Seventeen names, and that's the whole API

[`src/itsdangerous/__init__.py`](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/src/itsdangerous/__init__.py#L1-L17) is seventeen lines, each one an import re-exported under its own name. Nothing else. No initialisation, no registry, no configuration read from the environment. Import the package and you get:

- three encoding helpers — [`base64_decode`, `base64_encode`, `want_bytes`](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/src/itsdangerous/__init__.py#L1-L3);
- six exception types — [`BadData` through `SignatureExpired`](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/src/itsdangerous/__init__.py#L4-L9);
- eight classes that do the work — [`Serializer`, `HMACAlgorithm`, `NoneAlgorithm`, `Signer`, `TimedSerializer`, `TimestampSigner`, `URLSafeSerializer`, `URLSafeTimedSerializer`](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/src/itsdangerous/__init__.py#L10-L17).

That is a reviewable amount of surface. It also means there is no hidden entry point: if a behaviour matters to you, it is reachable from one of those seventeen names, or it is not reachable at all.

The re-exports use the `from X import Y as Y` form. That redundant-looking `as Y` is what marks a name as deliberately exported for type checkers, so downstream projects importing `from itsdangerous import Signer` type-check cleanly. It is a small signal that the author thought about which names are public.

## Two layers, and the docs pick one for you

Of the eight working classes, the ones you actually choose between fall into two layers. The project's own documentation states the split plainly: the signer is "the basic system that signs a given `bytes` value", and the serializer "wraps a signer to enable serializing and signing other data besides `bytes`" — and then it makes a recommendation: [**"Typically, you'll want to use a serializer, not a signer."**](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/concepts.rst#L5-L15)

This matters for review, because it tells you where the interesting code paths are. A `Signer` handles bytes and only bytes. A `Serializer` sits on top of it and turns your dict into bytes first. Everything else in the export list is a variation: `TimestampSigner` adds time to a signer, `TimedSerializer` adds time to a serializer, `URLSafeSerializer` changes how the bytes are packed. The chain has two links, and most applications only ever touch the top one.

So when you ask "what does this library guarantee," you are really asking about two contracts stacked on each other. We will get to both. First, the claim itself.

## The claim, stated by the project

The documentation's opening is not vague about what signing buys you:

> ["The receiver can see the data, but they can not modify it unless they also have your key. So if you keep the key secret and complex, you will be fine."](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/index.rst#L14-L20)

Read that twice, because both halves are load-bearing. *They can see the data.* This is tamper **detection**, not confidentiality. The library is not encrypting anything. It is attaching evidence that the data came from you.

The [README's example](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/README.md#L21-L32) demonstrates this without meaning to. It signs `{"id": 5, "name": "itsdangerous"}` and prints the token:

```
eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9.6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg
```

Everything before the dot is the payload. Decode that base64 and you get the JSON back. No key required. Anyone holding the token — the user, their browser extension, a proxy log, whoever found the email — can read the id and the name. That is not a flaw; it is the documented design. But it is the single most common misunderstanding about this library, and it is the first thing you should check for in any code you are signing off: *is there anything in this payload the token-holder shouldn't know?*

The documented use cases are consistent with this. All three — [an unsubscribe link, a cookie replacing a server-side session, server state round-tripped through a client](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/index.rst#L35-L47) — share the same shape: the data is *about* the recipient, so the recipient reading it costs nothing. What would cost something is the recipient *editing* it. That is the thing being prevented.

## One input holds everything up

There is exactly one secret in this design. The docs are direct about the consequences: ["Signatures are secured by the `secret_key`... If an attacker learns the secret key, they can change and resign data to look valid."](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/concepts.rst#L18-L29)

Three operational requirements follow from that passage, and they are the ones you will want to ask a team about:

1. **It must be long and random.** The docs say so explicitly and later suggest [`os.urandom`](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/concepts.rst#L49-L53) as a generator. The library will not stop you from passing `"secret"`.
2. **It must not be in source control.** The suggested pattern is [reading it from an environment variable](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/concepts.rst#L30-L42).
3. **Compromise has exactly one remedy** — change the key, which invalidates every token already issued. There is no revocation list, no per-token state. The docs state the invalidation consequence up front: ["Changing the secret key will invalidate existing tokens."](https://github.com/pallets/itsdangerous/blob/672971d66a2ef9f85151e53283113f33d642dabd/docs/concepts.rst#L21-L23)

The same passage drops a hint about structure that we will pick up shortly: *"Typically one secret key is used with all signers, and the salt is used to distinguish different contexts."* One key, many contexts, separated by something called a salt. Hold that thought.

## What we don't know yet

We have a claim — *readable, not modifiable* — and a single secret that backs it. We do not yet have the mechanism, and three questions about it decide whether the claim survives contact with reality.

**What is the signature actually computed over?** The README token has a payload and a tag separated by a dot. Is the tag over the payload alone? And the docs promise that a token signed for "activation" will not work for "upgrade" — that a user can't take one email link and use it as another. The word "salt" appears, but we have not seen what it does to the arithmetic. *(Chapter 4.)*

**What happens on failure?** When the bytes don't match, does the caller get an exception, a `False`, or — worse — a result that is partly trusted? You cannot reason about a library's safety until you know whether its failure mode is loud. *(Chapter 3, with the precise mechanics in chapter 5.)*

**Is any of the visible payload actually hidden?** The README suggests not, but a suggestion in a README is not a guarantee. We should look at the encoding functions and confirm that they are keyless and public — because if they are, the confidentiality question is settled permanently, for every class in the export list. *(Chapter 2, immediately.)*

That is the front door. Seventeen names, two layers, one secret, and a promise about modification rather than secrecy. Next we go one level down, to the bytes.

---

### What this chapter hands to the next

| | |
|---|---|
| **Characters** | the `itsdangerous` package namespace · `Signer` · `Serializer` · `URLSafeSerializer` · `TimestampSigner` · the secret key |
| **Facts** | the public API is exactly 17 re-exports and nothing else · two layers: `Signer` over bytes, `Serializer` over objects, and the docs steer you to the serializer · the guarantee is tamper detection, not confidentiality — "the receiver can see the data" · everything rests on one `secret_key`, which must be long, random, kept out of VCS, and changed on compromise · the README's own token shows a readable base64 payload |
| **Open questions** | *q1.1* What is the signature computed over, and what makes an "activation" token invalid for "upgrade"? *(ch. 4)* · *q1.2* On failure: exception, falsy value, or partial trust? *(ch. 3)* · *q1.3* Can anyone decode the payload without the key? *(ch. 2)* |

### Proof

This block runs against the real repository with `PYTHONPATH=src`. If the public surface or the readability of a token stops matching the story, it fails.

```python proof
import base64
import itsdangerous
from itsdangerous.serializer import Serializer
from itsdangerous.signer import Signer

# --- Fact: the public surface is exactly these 17 names, and nothing else. ---
expected = {
    "base64_decode", "base64_encode", "want_bytes",
    "BadData", "BadHeader", "BadPayload",
    "BadSignature", "BadTimeSignature", "SignatureExpired",
    "Serializer", "HMACAlgorithm", "NoneAlgorithm", "Signer",
    "TimedSerializer", "TimestampSigner",
    "URLSafeSerializer", "URLSafeTimedSerializer",
}
assert len(expected) == 17
public = {n for n in vars(itsdangerous) if not n.startswith("_")}
# Submodules become attributes once imported; ignore them, compare real exports.
import types
public = {n for n in public if not isinstance(getattr(itsdangerous, n), types.ModuleType)}
assert public == expected, public ^ expected

# --- Fact: two layers. Signer handles bytes; Serializer wraps a signer. ---
assert issubclass(Serializer.default_signer, Signer)
assert isinstance(Signer("k").sign(b"raw bytes"), bytes)
assert not issubclass(Serializer, Signer)   # not the same layer, it *wraps* one

# --- Fact (q1.3 preview): the payload of a real token is readable without the key. ---
auth_s = itsdangerous.URLSafeSerializer("secret key", "auth")
token = auth_s.dumps({"id": 5, "name": "itsdangerous"})
assert token == "eyJpZCI6NSwibmFtZSI6Iml0c2Rhbmdlcm91cyJ9.6YP6T0BaO67XP--9UzTrmurXSmg"

payload, _, signature = token.rpartition(".")
# Decoded by a stranger holding no key at all:
raw = base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload + "=" * (-len(payload) % 4))
assert raw == b'{"id":5,"name":"itsdangerous"}'
assert b"itsdangerous" in raw   # the "secret" data was never secret

# --- Fact: the round trip returns the object to a holder of the key. ---
assert auth_s.loads(token) == {"id": 5, "name": "itsdangerous"}

# --- Fact: the secret key is the whole of the security. A different key rejects. ---
other = itsdangerous.URLSafeSerializer("different key", "auth")
try:
    other.loads(token)
except itsdangerous.BadSignature:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a token must not verify under a different secret key")
```
